evidence_notes.finding: A five-role pipeline (Planner, Coder, Tester, Debugger, Critic) with mandatory sandboxed execution of every patch resolves 40.0% of SWE-bench Lite tasks versus 14.0% for a same-model single-agent baseline and 12.0% for ReAct. Ablations attribute the gain jointly to execution feedback (Tester-Debugger loop) and role decomposition, at roughly 2.7x the per-task API cost.
evidence_notes.quote: AGENTFORGEachieves 40.0% task resolution, outperforming the single-agent baseline by +26.0% and the ReAct baseline by +28.0%.

extraction.key_results: 40.0% resolve / 37.5% patch rate vs 14.0% / 12.5% single-agent and 12.0% / 11.0% ReAct. Ablation on 100 tasks: full 42%, w/o Critic 38%, w/o Debugger 31%, w/o Tester 28%, w/o Planner 19%, single-agent 14%. Retry gains saturate after N=2. Failure modes on 30 sampled failures: faulty localization 40.0%, ineffective patch generation 26.7%, cognitive deadlock (repeated identical failing attempts) 20.0%, environment/tooling 13.3%. Cost 13,600 input + 5,100 output tokens ($0.1445/task) vs $0.054 single-agent, about 2.7x.
extraction.limitations: Operates at file-level granularity and struggles with multi-file coordination; binary resolve metric does not capture partial correctness or regressions; results rely on a single base model (GPT-4o) with one sample per agent and a fixed retry budget; strict sandbox limits (512 MB, 0.5 CPU, 30 s, no network) bound achievable performance; Tester-generated tests are sometimes brittle, weakening the execution-feedback signal; deployment still requires human oversight, static analysis, and audit.

evidence_notes.finding: Role heterogeneity buys division of labour but raises interdependence, so specialized multi-agent systems become more sensitive to interface mismatches, cascading error propagation, and coordination overhead; the survey argues failure attribution is unsettled because the point where an anomaly becomes observable rarely coincides with its origin.
evidence_notes.quote: As role diversity increases, so does interdependence among agents, making the system more sensitive to interface mismatches, cascading errors, and coordination overhead.

extraction.framework: surveys 12+ frameworks incl. MetaGPT, AutoGen, AgentVerse, AutoAgents, CAMEL, Generative Agents, Puppeteer, MASFactory
extraction.key_results: Organizes the field into a four-stage 'LIFE' progression (Lay capability foundation, Integrate via collaboration, Find faults via attribution, Evolve via self-improvement) and formalizes dependencies between adjacent stages. Reports a design shift from homogeneous to heterogeneous role configurations and from static to dynamic role allocation; homogeneous agent teams get trapped in repeated self-consistency loops while heterogeneous ones incur interface mismatch and coordination overhead. Explicit text-based communication dominates but scales poorly: repeated broadcasting of long textual states creates token overhead, increases latency, and amplifies inconsistency when agents interpret shared context differently. Failure attribution challenges identified: the attribution target is defined inconsistently across studies; anomaly propagation is strongly coupled so observable failure point differs from true origin; fine-grained (step/module/type) attribution remains unreliable under long-horizon multi-role dependencies; and synthetic failure datasets built from templates or rule-based injection lack realism.
extraction.limitations: Secondary study with no new experiments; comparability across attribution methods is limited because input granularity, annotation targets, and evaluation criteria differ between primary studies; many dynamic-role systems are heuristic and do not learn when specialization helps versus when extra agents add noise; the cross-stage closed-loop agenda is proposed rather than validated.

evidence_notes.finding: As LLM and agentic code generation becomes abundant, verification rather than authorship becomes the rate-limiting activity; AI-generated defects are syntactically plausible but semantically flawed, so they evade superficial review and require layered hybrid verification pipelines plus accountable human oversight.
evidence_notes.quote: Unlike traditional defects, these failures often evade superficial review due to their syntactic plausibility.

extraction.key_results: Multivocal review of 23 studies synthesized into four pillars and a competency framework: intent articulation, systematic verification, multi-agent orchestration, and accountable human judgment. Argues verification should be treated as infrastructure rather than a discrete phase, combining LLM reasoning with static analysis, dynamic testing, and formal methods, since LLMs act as both generators and verifiers and can share correlated failure modes. Cites a two-phase controlled experiment with 151 professional developers where AI assistance gave a 30.7% median reduction in task completion time in Phase 1 but no significant difference in completion time or code quality in Phase 2 when other developers evolved the code without AI, concluding maintainability depends on surrounding process infrastructure rather than the generative model. Notes an 'AI drag' effect where assistants boost senior engineers but impose a productivity drag on early-in-career developers, and that no single agent configuration is universally optimal so orchestration must be adaptive. Roadmap covers verification-first lifecycles, prompt provenance standards, auditability, liability attribution, and longitudinal workforce studies.
extraction.limitations: Construct validity is weak because 'agentic workflow' and 'orchestration' lack accepted definitions; external validity is bounded by a narrow time window and source set in a fast-moving field, with evidence drawn mainly from controlled or large industrial contexts; internal validity varies because multivocal sources differ in rigor and include non-validated perspectives; the proposed transformation framework is synthetic and conceptual, and its practical effectiveness awaits longitudinal real-world validation.

evidence_notes.finding: A concept-paper review across the SDLC argues multi-agent specialization improves modularity, tool use, and parallelism, but that current SE benchmarks measure isolated tasks and therefore cannot assess the cooperative capabilities that multi-agent systems are supposed to provide.
evidence_notes.quote: Existing benchmarks have focused on individual SE tasks and exhibit limitations as SE projects grow in complexity.

extraction.framework: reviews CrewAI, LangGraph, Google ADK, AutoGen, n8n; protocols CNP, A2A, ANP, MCP; systems incl. MARE, SpecGen, PairCoder, CodeAgent, GPTLens, LLIFT, CoverUp, WhiteFox, GPTDroid, AgentFL, ChatRepair, AutoSD
extraction.agent_count: 2 to 6 across reviewed systems (e.g. PairCoder 2, CodeAgent 6)
extraction.benchmark: discusses HumanEval, GSM8K, PURE, PROMISE, BugBench, Tests4Py
extraction.baseline: single LLM / standalone prompting (e.g. AUTOFL single-agent fault localization)
extraction.key_results: Systematic review of LLM-based multi-agent systems across five SDLC stages (requirements engineering, code generation, static code checking, testing, debugging). Claimed multi-agent advantages: per-task specialization, independent upgradeability/modularity, complementary perspectives, superior tool use, and parallel execution. Reports MARE surpassing SOTA text-parser and logical-reasoning baselines by 15.4% on requirements tasks. Identifies five forward challenges: agents can only simulate generic roles (developer, product manager) and lack SE-specific expertise such as vulnerability detection or security auditing; human-agent coordination (intervention points, feedback mechanisms) is underexplored; SDLC-wide data beyond code is needed; computational cost must be reduced via distillation, lightweight fine-tuning, and fewer inter-agent iterations; and cooperative-capability benchmarks are missing.
extraction.limitations: Concept paper with no new empirical evaluation; the review of selected works is described as concise rather than exhaustive; comparative evaluation of multi-agent design patterns (planner-executor pairs, self-refinement loops, human-in-the-loop) and empirical evaluation across open-source and proprietary LLMs are deferred to future work; deployment concerns around reliability, privacy, dynamic agent discovery, and cost management are raised but not measured.

evidence_notes.finding: A three-agent closed loop (generation, execution/analysis, review/optimization) with sandboxed execution feedback raises statement coverage from 72.8% to 94.9% and valid executable tests from 64.1% to 89.3% over a single-pass LLM baseline, but the authors report non-deterministic LLM behavior, coordination latency, and context drift as persistent reliability threats.
evidence_notes.quote: Although agentic systems enhance adaptability, they remain subject to non-deterministic LLM behavior

extraction.framework: Agentic Testing Architecture (ATA); LangChain orchestration, Kubernetes, FAISS, RabbitMQ
extraction.benchmark: 8 open-source repositories plus 2 internal enterprise applications (~4,000 LoC per module), Python/Java/JavaScript/Node.js
extraction.baseline: single-pass static LLM (GPT-4o-mini) test generation without feedback loops
extraction.key_results: Mean statement coverage 72.8% -> 94.9% (+30.3%); branch coverage 61.5% -> 91.7% (+49.2%); valid executable tests 64.1% -> 89.3% (+39.3%); runtime per module 3.5 h -> 1.1 h (-68.6%); QA validation effort 11.8 -> 3.4 person-hours (-71.2%). Convergence typically at 4-6 iterations (Python) and 5-7 (Java), mean 5.2. Persistent cross-agent vector memory prevented reintroduction of prior failure contexts, a limitation the authors attribute to single-model setups. Abstract claims up to 60% reduction in invalid tests and 30% coverage improvement.
extraction.limitations: Non-deterministic LLM outputs undermine reproducibility, especially in regulated or safety-critical settings; computational footprint grows with agent count and feedback cycles, and cited work reports context synchronization degrading beyond four concurrent reasoning agents due to token overlap and memory contention; persistent shared memory introduces semantic/embedding drift requiring context pruning and rolling windows; human oversight is still needed to prevent overfitting and self-confirming bias loops; multi-agent reasoning chains obscure accountability, motivating embedded provenance metadata; bias in training data can cascade through the generation pipeline.

evidence_notes.finding: Iterative full-scope LLM auditing of a seven-lane multi-agent prompt-specification surface surfaced 51 defects over nine non-monotonic rounds; cross-lane data-contract defects were undetectable by single-file review by construction and only appeared once multi-file context loading was enabled.
evidence_notes.quote: By construction, single-file review cannot detect cross-lane data-contract issues; in this study every cross-lane defect surfaced only after multi-file context loading was enabled.

extraction.framework: AEGIS (Autonomous Engineering Governance and Intelligence System)
extraction.agent_count: 7 lanes (seven-lane production pipeline), audited by an LLM sub-agent inspector
extraction.benchmark: none standard; 7152-line eight-document specification surface plus a released public synthetic mini-specification with 5 seeded defects
extraction.baseline: single-file review and one-pass audit (described conceptually; a single-pass full-scope control was NOT run)
extraction.key_results: 51 consistency defects surfaced across nine rounds (per-round 15, 8, 12, 2, 8, 1, 4, 1, 0), converging non-monotonically; Mann-Kendall trend significant (p = 0.008, tau = -0.72) but reported descriptively due to round non-independence. Seven-category post hoc defect taxonomy with coding rules. Cascading edits observed: fixing a defect in round 5 created a newly incorrect changelog reference caught in round 6. Cross-LLM partial replication with four frontier vendors (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, xAI; 12 traces) found vendor blind spots were non-overlapping and the multi-vendor union detected all five seeded defects. Inter-rater reliability on a stratified 18-defect subsample: Cohen's kappa = 0.80 on category, 0.46 on severity. Automated verification greps caught structural issues but missed semantic drift.
extraction.limitations: Single system (n = 1) with no control group; the same LLM family (Claude) both authored and audited the specifications, so a clean pass shows internal consistency rather than ground-truth correctness; the seven-category taxonomy is post hoc, single-coder, and possibly non-exhaustive; sample sizes are modest (9 rounds, 51 defects) and rounds are not independent draws because audit scope expanded during the study; with a stochastic auditor and no repeat trials, the round-3 and round-5 bumps cannot be distinguished from auditor variance; the audit protocol co-evolved with discovered defects, so later prompts may be tuned to the known defect space and fix ordering may have shaped category progression; convergence to zero findings establishes internal consistency, not correctness; no single-pass full-scope control, no human-only or hybrid review, and no multi-system replication; operational outcomes of the fixes are out of scope.

evidence_notes.finding: Under a fixed LLM and identical tasks, framework-level architectural choices alone drive over 100x latency differences, up to 30% planning accuracy loss, and coordination success collapsing from above 90% to below 30%, indicating multi-agent behavior is governed by execution semantics and interface design rather than model quality.
evidence_notes.quote: Our results show that framework-level design choices alone can increase latency by over 100×, reduce planning accuracy by up to 30%, and lower coordination success from above 90% to below 30%.

extraction.framework: MAFBench evaluating LangGraph, n8n, Langflow, CrewAI, AutoGen, OpenAI SDK, Agno, OpenAgents, DeepMind Concordia
extraction.agent_count: single-agent and multi-agent settings; coordination evaluated at scaling agent population sizes
extraction.benchmark: MAFBench (unified suite integrating existing benchmarks for orchestration, memory, planning, specialization, coordination)
extraction.baseline: direct LLM call (orchestration latency measured as multiplier of direct LLM) and single-agent settings
extraction.key_results: Orchestration latency 1.3x to 117x direct LLM; throughput 8.9 req/s down to <0.01. Overall memory score 23.8% (best) vs 6.1% (worst); memory forgetting fails universally because frameworks lack explicit memory editing and dependency-aware deletion. Planning accuracy change ranges +15% to -30% with 1.2x to 30x runtime multiplier; free-form natural-language planning generally helps while schema-constrained planning is a primary source of failure and overhead, converting correct reasoning into parsing/execution failures especially for local open models. Specialization delta F1 from about 0 to +58: professional role labels do not activate domain reasoning, but expert-guided procedural conditioning delivers large gains. Coordination task success at large n ranges >90% to <30% and is governed by communication topology, not interaction rounds, tokens, or model capacity; limited-hop neighbor-based topologies do best locally, sparse long-path graphs fail global agreement at scale, and only dense broadcast-style connectivity consistently enables system-wide consensus. Six design principles plus ORCA, a step toward automated multi-agent architecture selection.
extraction.limitations: The underlying LLM is fixed to isolate architectural effects (planning is the exception, evaluated across multiple LLMs), so results characterize framework architecture rather than model behavior; MAFBench integrates existing benchmarks under a standardized pipeline rather than proposing new tasks, and existing benchmarks vary in format, assumptions, and protocols requiring re-engineering; identified open gaps include lack of controlled forgetting, dependency-aware revision, contradiction resolution, memory growth guarantees, lifecycle management and versioning for procedural expertise, and runtime guarantees on convergence, stability, and cost as agent populations scale.

evidence_notes.finding: Trace-aligned fault injection shows perturbations at inter-agent communication boundaries propagate more damagingly than equivalent perturbations at single LLM calls: in ChatDev a 1000 ms A2A delay produced 59.2x mean runtime amplification versus 48.1x for an LLM delay, and 1.295x vs 1.053x in a minimal two-agent demo.
evidence_notes.quote: Overall, these results highlight that in a multi-phase, message-heavy workflow, the runtime impact of small injected delays can be magnified dramatically

extraction.framework: llmmas-otel (OpenTelemetry tracing + fault injection), validated on a Planner->Coder demo and on ChatDev
extraction.agent_count: 2 (demo Planner/Coder); ChatDev multi-agent across design, coding, testing phases
extraction.benchmark: ProgramDev (30 tasks), 5 runs per task per condition
extraction.baseline: fault-free baseline run of the same workflow, structurally aligned with faulty runs
extraction.key_results: Defines a trace model spanning session, segment (workflow phase), agent step, A2A send/receive, tool call, and LLM call spans with a stable attribute vocabulary. Supports faults at three boundaries: A2A send (delay, drop, truncate), A2A receive (delay, drop), tool call (delay, not_installed, timeout, malformed_response), and LLM call (delay, rate_limit, timeout, network_error, malformed_response). Amplification (extra end-to-end runtime / injected delay): demo LLM delay mean 1.053 (median 1.036), demo A2A delay mean 1.295 (median 1.390); ChatDev LLM delay mean 48.1 (median 13.9), ChatDev A2A delay mean 59.2 (median 6.6). Fault injection is an overlay on the same span structure so baseline and faulty runs stay comparable.
extraction.limitations: Initial validation only, on one minimal demo workflow and one real system (ChatDev); fault injection currently covers just three runtime boundaries (A2A, LLM, tool) and does not yet include higher-level workflow, memory-related, or coordination faults; the tool provides no higher-level analysis such as paired-run differencing, trace summarization, root-cause ranking, or automated debugging reports, so users must inspect traces manually; large gap between demo and ChatDev median vs mean amplification indicates high run-to-run variance.

evidence_notes.finding: A four-agent testing framework reaches 55.0% differential defect detection on QuixBugs versus 37.5% for a same-model single-agent baseline, and the ablation attributes that 17.5-point advantage to role decomposition rather than to the dedicated diagnostic agent; the conventional unconditional criterion overstates detection by 35 points (90.0% vs 55.0%).
evidence_notes.quote: Role decomposition is supported: the single-agent condition, run with the same model and the same budget, detects 17.5 fewer points under the differential criterion.

extraction.framework: four-agent multi-agent testing framework (requirement analysis, test-case generation, sandboxed execution, defect detection) on GLM-4-Flash
extraction.baseline: same-model single-agent configuration of the same framework; also diagnosis-only and execution-only ablations
extraction.key_results: Differential detection (two-run protocol against reference implementation, recommended primary indicator) 55.0% (SD 3.1) vs 90.0% unconditional and 5.0% strict; the 35-point gap is traced to LLM test artifacts, mainly hallucinated oracle values and signature mismatches. Same-model single-agent baseline reaches 37.5% differentially (-17.5 points). Removing the diagnostic agent costs only 2.5 points differentially, within seed-to-seed variation, and diagnosis-only is the worst of four conditions; the composite rule's extra detections do not survive the differential check. Failure analysis: 9 of 18 differentially undetected programs get suites that execute and fail but fail identically on correct code (oracle quality), with input construction and path coverage accounting for the other 9. Cost about 9,300 tokens and 143 s per program.
extraction.limitations: Single benchmark (QuixBugs: 40 moderate-size single-line-fault programs), limiting generalization to industrial code with module interplay, race conditions, and specification-implementation mismatch; every detection occurred in the first round across all five runs so the iterative feedback loop is an architectural capability with no demonstrated empirical effectiveness on this benchmark; all conditions use one model (GLM-4-Flash) so framework effects cannot be separated from model effects; test quality assessed only via execution outcomes with no human evaluation of readability or maintainability; attribution categories in the failure table are lower bounds and the attributable count of nineteen is an upper bound; the only controlled comparison is against a single-agent configuration of the same framework, not against other architectures; the differential protocol requires a reference implementation that a live repository lacks; per-unit cost figures are a lower bound.

evidence_notes.finding: On HumanEval black-box unit-test generation, prompt engineering rather than architecture is the primary driver: multi-agent collaborative and competitive configurations achieve marginally higher coverage (peak 99.54%) but statistically comparable execution success to a single agent (96.98% vs 96.89%) while consuming 3-4x the tokens.
evidence_notes.quote: Although multi-agent architectures achieve superior test coverage — peaking at 99.54% — they yield an ESR comparable to single-agent frameworks (96.98% versus 96.89%).

extraction.framework: extended QA Agent framework (Deo et al.) with collaborative Merge/Concat and Competitive LLM-scorer patterns; base model nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b
extraction.agent_count: multiple (single-agent baseline vs multi-agent collaborative and competitive configurations, incl. a Code Architect role)
extraction.benchmark: HumanEval (full 164 problems and a curated 20-problem harder subset), 10 independent runs
extraction.baseline: single-agent LLM configuration under the same prompting strategy; also GPT-4 Turbo QA Agent and AgentCoder reference results
extraction.key_results: Rule-augmented few-shot prompting improves coverage and Execution Success Rate by 20-30% over zero-shot across all architectures. Single-agent with rule-augmented few-shot: ESR 96.98%, coverage 99.30% on the full dataset, at minimum token cost, versus ESR 62.17% / coverage 68.23% zero-shot. Best multi-agent (Merge Concat, rule-augmented few-shot): ESR 96.41%, coverage 99.54%. Multi-agent gains are largest under plain few-shot (ESR up to +5.56% curated, +2.91% full; coverage up to +2.19% curated, +3.21% full) and shrink under rule-augmented prompting. On the harder curated subset multi-agent always beat single-agent; on the easier full dataset a single agent matched or exceeded it. Multi-agent costs roughly 3-4x the single-agent token volume, a non-proportional increase for marginal accuracy gains.
extraction.limitations: Only a single benchmark dataset (HumanEval) is used, which the authors state is the main threat to external validity; curated-subset results are unexpectedly higher than full-dataset results, possibly because of affinity between selected tasks and the few-shot examples; the isolated effect of adding rules without few-shot examples was not measured; performance variation across task difficulty was not analyzed in depth; the reference-work comparison uses a different (stronger) base model; no critic agent or iterative feedback loop is included in the tested architectures.

evidence_notes.finding: A tri-role multi-agent pipeline (Evaluator, Student Simulator, Reviewer) produced the highest composite quality (CQS 4.21/5) and lowest over-praise and hallucination rates, but consumed roughly 4.6x the tokens of a zero-shot single agent, while a chain-of-thought single agent reached 86.5% of the top score at 32.5% of its token cost.
evidence_notes.quote: The S4 strategy consumed approximately 4.6 times the tokens of S1, translating to proportionally higher API costs.

extraction.framework: four prompting configurations (S1 zero-shot single-agent, S2 chain-of-thought single-agent, S3 dual-role draft+critique, S4 tri-role Evaluator/Student Simulator/Reviewer) on GPT-4-Turbo
extraction.benchmark: 200 undergraduate argumentative essays; multi-dimensional rubric (accuracy, specificity, actionability, constructive tone, completeness) scored by 3 trained raters plus automated similarity to expert reference feedback
extraction.key_results: Multi-agent configurations outperformed single-agent across all five rubric dimensions; S4 achieved the highest composite quality score (CQS = 4.21 on a 5-point scale) and the lowest rates across all four error categories (over-praise, over-inference, hallucination, omission). The multi-agent advantage is not uniform: stratified by instructor pre-score quartile, the S4-over-S2 CQS gap was 0.74 points for second-quartile essays but narrowed to 0.38 for top-quartile essays, indicating the largest incremental value where diagnostic complexity is highest. Mean tokens per feedback instance: S1 847, S2 1,264, S3 2,531, S4 3,892 (S4 about 4.6x S1). S2 delivers 86.5% of S4's CQS at 32.5% of its token cost, and S3 is proposed as a cost/quality compromise.
extraction.limitations: Single LLM (GPT-4-Turbo), so generalization to Claude, Gemini, or open-source families requires cross-model replication; the essay corpus comes from a single institution and a single discipline (English academic writing), limiting ecological breadth; only three human raters were used; feedback quality was evaluated as a static property of one interaction with no longitudinal measurement of student revision gains; no cross-disciplinary replication and no student perception or think-aloud data.

evidence_notes.finding: A deterministic validation agent wrapped in a bounded generate-validate-regenerate loop acts as a robustness amplifier that homogenizes output quality across ten heterogeneous LLM backends, so models differ mainly in first-attempt stability and latency rather than in ultimate ability to satisfy the specification.
evidence_notes.quote: Even for models with imperfect first-attempt behavior, the combination of deterministic validation and bounded regeneration significantly increases the final success rate.

extraction.framework: modular multi-agent text-to-diagram pipeline (Agent 3 meta-selector, Agent 5 synthesizer, Agent 7 deterministic validator, Agent 9 user-guided refiner)
extraction.benchmark: 30 prompts (20 easy, 10 complex) x 10 LLMs = 300 runs; metrics are final validation success, first-attempt success, validation iterations, error profile, latency
extraction.baseline: monolithic / single-pass single-model text-to-diagram generation (conceptual comparison)
extraction.key_results: On easy prompts most models reach 95-100% final success with high first-attempt rates; on complex prompts several models reach 100% final success but 0% first-attempt (kimi-k2-thinking, gpt-5-codex, grok-code-fast-1), while glm-4.6 and grok-4-fast reach 0% final success. Agent 7 error profiling separates syntax_errors, missing_nodes/missing_edges, invalid_attributes, style_violations, and other; non-successful runs are dominated by syntax errors with structural errors nearly absent, indicating that once syntax is correct the structural semantics usually match the specification. Style/flavor violations are rare, so stylistic guidance integrates without destabilizing structural correctness. Latency varies significantly across providers, creating a speed-versus-stability trade-off for interactive tools.
extraction.limitations: Only ten runs per model on the complex prompt set, which the author says should be interpreted with caution; benchmarks are largely flowchart- and ER-style diagrams, so broader complex specifications remain untested; no formal statistical testing or threats-to-validity section; semantic grounding via DSLs and graph-transformation backends, multimodal inputs, provenance, safety, and usability studies are all deferred to future work.

evidence_notes.finding: Across 94 papers on LLM-based multi-agent systems for SE, Role-Based Cooperation is the dominant design pattern (44 systems, 47.4%) among 16 identified patterns, chosen mainly to improve functional correctness and modularity, while performance efficiency (51.1%) and maintainability (50.0%) are traded off against each other.
evidence_notes.quote: Role-Based Cooperation is the design pattern most frequently employed among 16 patterns used to construct LLM-based MASs

extraction.framework: 94 LLM-based MASs incl. MetaGPT, MARE, MAAD, AgileCoder, AgentFL, FixAgent, CODER, INTERVENOR
extraction.agent_count: varies across the 94 surveyed systems (e.g. MAAD 4 role-dedicated agents, AgentFL 4 roles, planner/developer/reviewer triads)
extraction.benchmark: discusses DevBench and notes absence of a lifecycle-wide benchmark
extraction.key_results: Ten SE tasks identified with Code Generation most common; Functional Suitability is the most-considered quality attribute, with Functional Correctness explicitly targeted by 91.5% of systems; 16 design patterns identified with Role-Based Cooperation used by 44 (47.4%); the most common design rationale is Improving the Quality of Generated Code (44.7%), followed by Simulating Human Processes of Solving SE Tasks (29.8%), Optimizing Software Resource Management (28.7%), and Improving the Efficiency of Software Artifact Generation (24.5%). Performance Efficiency is considered by 51.1% and Maintainability by 50.0%, with 22.3% considering both; Modularity is the most frequent Maintainability sub-QA and is chiefly pursued via Role-Based Cooperation. End-to-End Software Maintenance (8.4%) and End-to-End Software Development (7.4%) remain rare, attributed to missing lifecycle-wide evaluation criteria, missing standard benchmarks for most development stages, and difficulty keeping artifact formats and semantics consistent across stages. Cites an empirical finding that one-pass and multi-pass prompting show no apparent output-quality difference while one-pass consumes fewer API calls.
extraction.limitations: Construct validity is threatened because data collection and extraction were manual and subject to individual bias, mitigated only by a pilot extraction; internal validity is not discussed since the study involves no experimental manipulation and supports no causal inference; findings describe what designers report rather than measured system outcomes, so pattern prevalence is not evidence of pattern effectiveness; open challenges noted include mismatches between user expectations and agent capabilities, ambiguities in communication protocols, and limited methods for validating results and quality of inter-agent interactions.

evidence_notes.finding: Across five coordination strategies and four 7-8B open-source models, a single-agent baseline with the best-matched model in few-shot mode outperformed every multi-agent alternative (recall 100%, precision 70.4%, F1 82.6%, WSS@95 43.4%), indicating model selection outweighs coordination strategy at this parameter scale.
evidence_notes.quote: Multi-agent strategies introduced coordination overhead without measurable benefit under the conditions of this study.

extraction.framework: PaSSER-SR platform with five strategies: S1 single-agent, S2 majority voting, S3 recall-focused OR ensemble, S4 confidence-weighted aggregation, S5 two-stage screening with debate; blockchain-verified audit trail (private Antelope chain, OpenTimestamps, Zenodo)
extraction.agent_count: 1 to 3 (single agent; 3-model ensembles; gate model plus 2-model debate panel)
extraction.benchmark: Gold Standard of 200 papers (190 for evaluation) from a 2,036-record corpus on blockchain-based e-voting; 25 GS configurations plus 5 full-corpus configurations
extraction.baseline: single-agent (S1) screening with each of Mistral 7B, LLaMA 3.1 8B, Granite 3.3 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B in zero-shot and few-shot modes
extraction.key_results: Best configuration is S1 with Qwen 2.5 7B few-shot: recall 100.0%, precision 70.4%, F1 82.6%, WSS@95 43.4%, beating all multi-agent alternatives (ranks 2-5 were S5 76.2, S5 75.8/74.5, S2 75.1, S4 75.1 F1). S2 and S4 produced identical results across all metrics, so self-reported confidence from 7-8B models adds no discriminative value. S5 filtered up to 38.4% of papers in stage 1 (about 18% inference saving) but did not improve precision; S3 amplified false positives without recall gains. Multi-agent screening introduced no new error types: no paper was a false positive only under a multi-agent strategy, and a persistent pool of 28 false positives (19 of them EC3 'no original contribution' surveys/position papers) appeared in all five full-corpus configurations, indicating a precision ceiling. Only two false negatives occurred overall, both under single-agent S1. Models that actively cited exclusion criteria (Qwen: 248/365 citations, 25/29 FPs) outperformed keyword-matching models (Granite: 0 citations, 121 FPs). Ranking was stable between Gold Standard and full corpus.
extraction.limitations: Validated on a single, deliberately terminologically overloaded domain (blockchain-based e-voting), so results are domain-specific; the 200-paper Gold Standard (190 evaluated) limits statistical power and the 95% Wilson precision intervals overlap across the top five configurations; few-shot calibration examples were drawn from the same corpus, a possible indirect data leakage despite excluding the 10 calibration papers; all models are 4-bit quantised 7-8B variants on consumer hardware and the authors hypothesize larger models may benefit more from coordination, citing API-model evidence of multi-agent gains at higher parameter scales; human inter-rater agreement was only kappa = 0.515, introducing ground-truth uncertainty, and results were not reported separately for agreed versus disputed labels.
